passages.title: Passage I — Alex Atala and Brazilian Cuisine

paras.t: At first,

Brazilian chef Alex Atala opened his restaurant in São Paulo in 1999, people told him he would never succeed. In a country where European cuisine was held in the highest regard, they said, no one would patronize a restaurant serving Brazilian food. Atala, whose restaurant has consistently ranked among the world's best, has long disproven the naysayers. Using traditional Brazilian
ingredients, such as, manioc root
and even ants—in innovative ways, he has
thrilled
diners from around the world.
Still, Atala felt he could do more for his country and its cuisine.

In 2012, he founded Instituto Atá to help promote lesser-known ingredients, particularly those of the Amazon basin, while working to protect Brazil's biodiversity. Hearts of palm, for example, were typically harvested from Brazil's wild juçara palms in an unsustainable way. Needing eight years to mature, the
tree dies once its
large heart is removed. Atala began persuading producers to cultivate Amazonian pupunha palms, which grow clusters of stems, each with a small heart. Careful harvesting ensures that the tree will
live to yield
more hearts, resulting in environmentally friendly production.
Atala prioritizes his working relationships with Amazonian tribes. Utilizing their historical
know-how they have,
he aims to bolster tribe members' livelihoods while exposing a wider audience to Brazilian ingredients. For instance, Baniwa women have farmed distinctly flavorful chili peppers for
centuries that use
indigenous agricultural techniques, to create a seasoning called pimenta jiquitaia. Partnering with Instituto Atá
have enabled
these women from a remote rain forest region to scale up production and market their product globally.
Expanding awareness of the rich diversity of Brazil's native ingredients, Atala continues to lead in
deciphering
the country's food culture. With his characteristic passion and intensity, the renowned chef seeks to inspire Brazilians to rediscover the connections between culture, nature, and food.
Hrosvitha, a medieval
author and dramatist—is

one of the earliest known European women playwrights. Although little is known about her life, scholars agree Hrosvitha was born to a noble family around 935 CE. As a relation of Holy Roman Emperor Otto I, she most likely spent her early years as part of his court. Later, sometime before 959 CE, she entered
the abbey at Gandersheim, it was well known
as a significant center of learning.

Hrosvitha entered Gandersheim as a canoness rather than a nun. Her title did not require a vow of poverty, but Hrosvitha did take the abbey's customary vow of chastity, which absolved her of an obligation to marry. This circumstance
made it okay for her to keep
her financial status without incurring responsibilities to a husband and children.
Nevertheless,
Hrosvitha had a greater level of independence—she could acquire property, receive guests, employ servants, and visit the royal court—than most women of her time.
Hrosvitha produced at least eight narrative religious poems, two historical epics
(about the court of Otto I and
Gandersheim), and six comedy-dramas. It is for these dramas that she is best known today.
Every night while driving home from a hectic day at work, my three-year-old twins quarreling in the backseat, I take a short detour. I turn off the gridlocked
highway, onto a stretch of Route 66 that is,
surrounded by arid New Mexico hills. When we're nearly three miles into our detour, I roll down the windows. Looking pointedly
into the rearview mirror, windows rolled down,
I say something about not throwing anything out of the car, but neither boy is listening. I check my speed.
Carefully, I steer toward the fog line. “Here it is, boys!” I yell at the backseat, the passenger-side tires finding the rumble strips etched into the asphalt.
Normal rumble strips create that loud, grating noise when you drive over them—
like a built-in alarm for drivers who drift too close to the road's edge.

These strips are different. The boys abruptly stop their squalling as the car begins to vibrate. Then, instead of that jolting warning noise, we hear the distinct strain of the song “America the Beautiful.”
The road is playing us a song.
I've been taking this detour out of Albuquerque for two years, ever since these musical rumble strips
were installed.

City planners wanted to find out whether the novelty of hearing a snippet of song would give drivers an incentive to obey the speed limit; the tune is only recognizable if they're going a reasonable forty-five miles per hour. Whether this strategy works, I don't know.

For me, this brief musical interlude is a charming curiosity, a welcome interruption in my work-week slog. Even though constant traffic has worn down the musical rumble strips and warped the sound of some of the notes,
there are currently no plans to restore the strips.
After the last one of the notes
fades
into the darkening sky, I glance back at the boys,
who have
been lulled by the wonder of the song.
I stop worrying about work, about how many toy cars might have gotten lost between there and home.
Until then,
I feel like everything is going to be just fine.

passages.title: Passage IV — The Case for Visible Storage

paras.t: Public museums exist for two main reasons: to educate the public and provide stewardship
(legal and ethical management, care, documentation, and use)
of their collections. Unfortunately, due to space constraints, a typical museum only exhibits about ten percent of the items in its collection; the other ninety percent remains in storage.
When displaying

such a small portion of artifacts severely limits public access and therefore public education. Furthermore, maintaining such a large number of artifacts in storage while acquiring additional items makes finding enough suitable storage space difficult, especially for delicate items.
To remain true to the goals of education and stewardship, museums should dedicate public access space to visible storage.
Also known as open storage, visible
storage provides
ways to display many items in small or irregular spaces, allowing more artifacts to be on exhibit.
In a traditional museum display, each artifact is labeled and positioned at eye level with plenty of space
between it
and the other objects.
Subsequently,

artifacts in visible storage spaces are placed close together and are often displayed from floor to ceiling with few labels. Areas of a museum that cannot house a traditional display, therefore, might be ideal for a visible storage display. Ceramic pottery
where it

might otherwise be positioned in individual glass cases might be lined up on shelves behind a glass wall. An antique fork and spoon fastened to a large informational board might instead be part of an entire set of silverware arranged under glass in pull-out cabinet drawers.
While some artifacts can never be displayed
, many pieces that
can—and should—
be viewed are not.
Whereas

a museum designates areas for visible storage, it uses space efficiently, providing safe displays for artifacts and allowing visitors greater access to independently study the works that make the museum unique.

passages.title: Passage V — The Sociable Weavers' Complex Nest

paras.t: In the sparse yet relatively green environment of the Kalahari Desert, birds known as sociable weavers build their enormous nests atop the desert's signature camelthorn trees. Slung across the branches, each nest—which can measure up to thirteen feet wide and seven feet thick—is a sprawling community home to hundreds of birds.
A weaver nest does not resemble a common bowl-like bird nest. Although the weavers use typical materials such as sticks, grass, and feathers to construct their nests, the nests look more like
disorganized piles.
Built within each nest are as many as one hundred four-to-six-inch-wide chambers. A bird enters a chamber by flying to the underside of the nest,
it squeezes
through a one-inch-wide entrance hole, and continuing up a passageway to a chamber. In each chamber, up to five of the sparrow-sized birds can huddle
as a group together when the Kalahari nights get cold.
The multi-chamber construction of the weaver nest has drawn comparisons to that of an apartment building. Indeed, the nests exemplify communal living
at there
most effective. Each one houses multiple generations of birds, all of whom work together to maintain their home.

passages.title: Passage VI — The Artful Stitch of Paj Ntaub

paras.t: She depicts flowers with layers of petals, intricate spirals and rosettes, teardrops bending within circles, and
dizzying mazes of lines—

embroidering them in vibrant reds, blues, pinks, yellows, and greens on fabric of delicate silk or cotton. Pang Xiong Sirirathasuk Sikoun is a master of paj ntaub, or “flower cloth” embroidery, the most difficult of the
century's-oldest
Hmong needlework arts.
Paj ntaub is increasingly made in lighter, softer shades today.

She's been creating stitched textiles since she was a young woman living in northern Laos. For the past several decades, she's been designing paj ntaub in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where she also teaches her craft.
Flower cloth
(commonly as a shirt, dress, coat, or collar)
is made to be worn as clothing and, depending on the amount of needlework on the piece, is designed either for everyday wear or for a special occasion.
With pattern names such as “elephant's foot” and “snail house” and images of animals framed by geometric designs,
paj ntaub patterns are versatile.
What distinguishes paj ntaub from other Hmong needlework arts are the artist's use of tiny, tight stitches and several complex techniques. One technique is reverse
appliqué, in which
shapes are cut out from, rather than added on top of, the embroidered fabric. Another is elaborate overstitching: thousands of layered stitches are applied to
its surface.
Pang Xiong regrets that most people she knows today wear only
regular
clothes. When she was growing up in Laos, she explains, she had few items of clothing, but each garment she owned was handcrafted paj ntaub.
However,

she still wears flower cloth every day and would like to inspire others to do so. Pang Xiong teaches paj ntaub in art museums—including at the Smithsonian Institution, where some of her textiles are on permanent display—and in community settings around Philadelphia.
Pang Xiong is showing a new generation the joys of paj ntaub and beautiful handcrafted clothing.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The opening “At first, Brazilian chef … people told him” lacks a subordinator. “When” turns the first part into a dependent clause: “When Atala opened …, people told him.” “Years ago” leaves it a fragment.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The dashes already set off the inserted list, so the list must read “ingredients—such as manioc root … and even ants—in innovative ways.” Option B matches the dash structure; C and D misplace the punctuation.

questions.stem: The writer wants to emphasize the positive experience diners have had at Atala's restaurant. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
questions.explain: The goal is to emphasize a *positive* dining experience. “Thrilled” is positive; “mystified,” “shocked,” and “startled” are all negative or neutral.

questions.stem: Given that all the choices are accurate, which one provides the best transition from the preceding paragraph to this paragraph?
options: Atala is known for sometimes incorporating fragrances into his dishes as well.
In fact, Atala's culinary training took place in classic European restaurants.
Atala's obvious affection for his homeland is said to be infectious.
questions.explain: The passage moves from his restaurant success to his work for Brazil. “Atala's obvious affection for his homeland is said to be infectious” bridges the two paragraphs and motivates the transition to Instituto Atá.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “The tree dies once its large heart is removed” — “tree” is singular, and “its” is the correct possessive (no apostrophe). “It's” means “it is,” which is wrong here.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively maintains the essay's tone?
questions.explain: “Live to yield more hearts” is formal and consistent with the essay's register. “Churn out,” “doling out,” and “pull through and spawn” are too casual and colloquial.

questions.stem: Which choice is least redundant in context?
options: knowledge that tribe members know about local plants,
knowledge of local plants in the area,
questions.explain: “Know-how they have” is redundant. “Knowledge of local plants” removes the redundancy and the modifier confusion; B and C add unnecessary restatement.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The peppers themselves do not “use” techniques — the women do. “Centuries, using indigenous agricultural techniques” correctly attaches the action to the farmers.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The subject is the singular gerund phrase “Partnering with Instituto Atá,” so the verb must be singular: “has enabled.” (“Women” sits in a prepositional phrase and is not the subject.)

questions.stem: Which choice is clearest and most precise in context?
questions.explain: “Deciphering” (interpreting) the food culture is precise here. “Transforming,” “dislocating,” and “contorting” imply an unwanted distortion.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “Hrosvitha, a medieval author and dramatist, is one of the earliest …” — the appositive must be set off by a comma after it. The em-dash in the original leaves the “is” orphaned.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: Gandersheim and, historically, this abbey was
questions.explain: The original joins two independent clauses with a comma — a comma splice. “She entered the abbey at Gandersheim, an abbey well known as a significant center of learning” makes “an abbey” an appositive, eliminating the splice.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively maintains the essay's tone?
options: permitted her to hang on to
questions.explain: The register is formal historical prose. “Allowed her to retain” is the formal, precise phrasing. “Okay for her to keep,” “hang on to,” and “keep up” are too casual.

questions.stem: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?
questions.explain: “Nevertheless” signals a contrast: despite the restriction (vow of chastity), she enjoyed greater independence than most women. B and D restate the same contrast; C (causation) is wrong because no cause–effect link is intended.

questions.stem: Which choice best helps indicate that each historical epic covered different subject matter?
options: (each focused on the court of Otto I and
(focusing on the court of Otto I as well as
(one about the court of Otto I, the other about
questions.explain: The goal is to show each epic covered *different* subject matter. Only “(one about the court of Otto I, the other about Gandersheim)” clearly separates the two subjects; the others ambiguously combine them.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: highway onto a stretch of Route 66, that is,
highway onto a stretch, of Route 66 that is
highway onto a stretch of Route 66 that is
questions.explain: “I turn off the gridlocked highway onto a stretch of Route 66 that is surrounded by arid New Mexico hills.” The commas in the original interrupt the flow; D removes the misplaced commas.

questions.stem: Which choice is least redundant in context?
options: into the rearview mirror, three miles into our detour,
behind me by looking into the rearview mirror,
questions.explain: “Windows rolled down” was already stated earlier in the sentence. “Into the rearview mirror” alone is the least redundant.

questions.stem: If the writer were to delete the underlined portion (adjusting the punctuation as needed), the paragraph would primarily lose:
options: information that indicates how prevalent rumble strips are on roadways.
a detail that reveals the narrator's opinion of distracted drivers.
information that clarifies a primary function of rumble strips.
a detail that indicates what the rumble strips look like.
questions.explain: The deleted phrase explains what rumble strips *do* — warn drivers. Removing it loses that function-clarifying information. It does not address prevalence, the narrator's opinion, or appearance.

questions.stem: Which choice is least redundant in context?

were added a couple years ago.
questions.explain: “Were installed” is concise and adds no redundancy. B, C, and D restate information already given (Albuquerque location, music, timing).

questions.stem: Given that all the choices are accurate, which one most effectively leads into the rest of the essay?
options: lots of other drivers, not just me, still make this detour to hear the tune.
sometimes drivers will turn around and drive over the strips again.
this detour on our drive home never fails to buoy my spirits.
questions.explain: The essay turns personal at the end (riding the music, feeling better about work and home). “This detour on our drive home never fails to buoy my spirits” leads directly into that personal, reflective close. The others introduce other drivers and dilute the narrator's focus.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The subject is “the last one” (singular), so the verb “fades” is correct. “Fade,” “disappear,” and “have disappeared” are plural or mismatched.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “The boys, who have been lulled” — “who” is the subject of the clause (they have been lulled), not “whom” (object). “Whose” and “they have” do not fit.

questions.stem: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?
questions.explain: “For now, I feel like everything is going to be just fine” conveys a present, momentary calm. “Until then,” “Now and then,” and “Later” do not fit the reflective present moment.

questions.stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following accurate sentence: *I hear there is another musical road in the US, somewhere in California.* Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it makes clear that the narrator has plans to travel on other musical roads.
Yes, because it indicates that the musical road in New Mexico is not unique.
No, because it draws the focus away from the New Mexico musical road and its effect on the narrator.
No, because it fails to provide specific details about the construction of the musical road in California.
questions.explain: Adding a fact about a California road would shift focus away from the New Mexico road and its personal effect on the narrator. The correct “No” reason is that it draws focus away — not the construction-detail reason in D.

questions.stem: *Question 25 asks about the preceding passage as a whole.* The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *It is marvelously quiet.* The sentence would most logically be placed at:
questions.explain: “It is marvelously quiet” fits Point A in Paragraph 1, where the narrator describes the calm detour before the music begins. Points B, C, and D come after the music or once the reflective mood has begun.

questions.stem: If the writer were to delete the underlined portion, the essay would primarily lose a:
options: suggestion that not all public museums provide proper stewardship for their artifacts.
clarification of what public museum stewardship entails.
list of reasons for educating the public on stewardship.
description of the daily tasks performed by curators.
questions.explain: The parenthetical defines what stewardship entails (management, care, documentation, use). Deleting it loses that clarification. It is not a suggestion about museums failing, a reason list, or a curator job description.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The original “When displaying … severely limits” is a fragment (missing its subject). “Displaying such a small portion of artifacts severely limits” turns it into a proper sentence with a gerund subject.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “Also known as open storage, visible storage provides ways to display many items …” is grammatically complete. B, C, and D create an error (awkward verb phrase or comma issue).

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “Each artifact is labeled and positioned … with plenty of space between it and the other objects” — “it” correctly refers to the singular “each artifact.” The plural pronouns in B and C do not match; D is wrong.

questions.stem: Which transition word is most logical in context?
questions.explain: The previous sentence describes the traditional display; this one contrasts with visible storage (close together, few labels). “Conversely” signals that contrast.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “Ceramic pottery that might otherwise be positioned in individual glass cases might be lined up …” — “that” correctly introduces the restrictive clause. “Where” is wrong for an object; “that which” and deletion are awkward.

questions.stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following parenthetical phrase: *(whether because of light sensitivity or the request of a donor)* Given that the information is accurate, should the writer make this addition here?
options: Yes, because it gives specific examples to help explain why some objects can never be displayed in a museum.
Yes, because it offers specific examples of items that require special storage.
No, because it detracts from the paragraph's focus on the ideal museum layout.
No, because it diminishes the role museums play in educating the public.
questions.explain: The parenthetical gives specific, relevant examples (light sensitivity, donor request) explaining *why* some things can never be displayed. B misstates it as examples of special-storage *items*; C and D misread the focus.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “Many pieces that can—and should—be viewed” correctly uses a matching pair of em-dashes. B drops the closing dash; C and D mix commas with dashes, violating consistency.

questions.stem: Which choice is clearest and most precise in context?
questions.explain: “When a museum designates areas for visible storage, it uses space efficiently” states a condition and its result. “Whereas” and “Although” imply concession; “Since” links vaguely without the condition–result clarity.

questions.stem: *Question 35 asks about the preceding passage as a whole.* The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *This potentially compromises stewardship.* For the sake of logic and cohesion, the sentence should be placed at:
questions.explain: “This potentially compromises stewardship” belongs at Point A in Paragraph 1, right after the discussion of storage problems (space limits, only 10% displayed). Points B, C, and D shift away from that first-paragraph claim.

questions.stem: If the writer were to delete the phrase “which can measure up to thirteen feet wide and seven feet thick” from the preceding sentence (adjusting the punctuation as needed), the sentence would primarily lose:
options: specific information that illustrates the minimum height at which the weavers begin building their nests.
specific information that underscores the enormousness of the weavers' nests.
details that clarify how the weavers are able to survive in the Kalahari Desert.
details that explain how the weavers' nests differ from other birds' nests.
questions.explain: The phrase gives the nests' size (thirteen feet wide, seven feet thick), which underscores their enormousness. The other options misstate what the phrase conveys.

questions.stem: The writer wants to emphasize the unusual appearance of the weavers' nests by using playful language to evoke a specific image. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
questions.explain: The goal is playful language evoking a specific image. “Carelessly plunked-down haystacks” vividly and playfully captures the sprawling, messy look. A, C, and D are neutral rather than playful.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The original is a comma splice (“… the nest, it squeezes”). The intended parallel list is “flying …, squeezing …, and continuing …” — “squeezing” matches “flying” and “continuing.”

options: all together, staying warm when the temperature drops and gets colder at night.
and stay warm when temperatures plummet at night and it's cold.
for warmth during the cold Kalahari nights.
questions.explain: “As a group together” is redundant. “For warmth during the cold Kalahari nights” is the concise, complete fix. B and C still contain redundancy or overstatement.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “The nests exemplify communal living at its most effective” — “its” is the correct possessive (no apostrophe). A keeps the misspelled “there”; B and C use “it's” (it is), which is wrong.

questions.stem: Which choice best maintains the stylistic pattern of descriptions established earlier in the sentence?
questions.explain: The sentence lists noun phrases (“flowers with layers …, intricate spirals …, teardrops …, and dizzying mazes of lines”). “Dizzying mazes of lines” matches the noun-phrase pattern; B, C, and D break it.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “Centuries-old” is a compound adjective — no apostrophe. “Century's-old,” “centuries'-old,” and “century's-oldest” are all malformed.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
options: Kept, because it compares Pang Xiong's embroidery style with that of modern paj ntaub.
Kept, because it places the subject of the essay in a modern context.
Deleted, because it detracts from the paragraph's focus on the various styles of ancient Hmong needlework arts.
Deleted, because it adds a detail that is irrelevant to the paragraph's introduction of Pang Xiong's connection to paj ntaub.

questions.stem: The best placement for the underlined portion would be:
questions.explain: “Flower cloth … is made to be worn as clothing …” — the parenthetical “(commonly as a shirt, dress, coat, or collar)” best fits right after “clothing,” since it specifies the examples of clothing. It is awkward where it currently sits.

options: only a master artist is able to create paj ntaub clothing for special occasions.
paj ntaub patterns are extraordinarily colorful.
paj ntaub celebrates the natural world.
questions.explain: The sentence lists pattern names (“elephant's foot,” “snail house”) and images of animals framed by geometric designs — a nature theme. “Paj ntaub celebrates the natural world” builds on that theme. A, B, and C do not connect to the animal and nature imagery.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “Reverse appliqué, in which shapes are cut out” — “in which” is the correct relative phrase and needs the comma. B loses the comma; C and D change the meaning.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: “Thousands of layered stitches are applied to its surface” — “its” correctly refers to the paj ntaub (singular). “Their surface” (D) mismatches number; B and C introduce ambiguous reference.

questions.stem: The writer is considering revising the underlined portion to the following: *mass-produced* Should the writer make this revision?
options: Yes, because the revision creates a clearer contrast between the homogeneous styles of clothing that are popular today and the handcrafted paj ntaub.
Yes, because the revision emphasizes Pang Xiong's desire for her handcrafted paj ntaub to be sold on a large scale in stores.
No, because the original word reinforces the idea that although paj ntaub clothing can be used for everyday wear, it should be saved for special occasions.
No, because the original word more specifically describes the type of clothing Pang Xiong disapproves of.
questions.explain: The revision to “mass-produced” should be made, because it creates a clear contrast between today's homogeneous, mass-produced clothing and Pang Xiong's handcrafted paj ntaub. B misreads her desire; C and D misread the original “regular.”

questions.stem: Which transition word or phrase, if any, is most logical in context?
questions.explain: “However” correctly signals a contrast: she regrets that others wear only “regular” clothes, yet *she* still wears flower cloth daily. “For example” and “Besides” do not fit the contrast; “She” drops the needed transition.

questions.stem: Which of the following true statements, if added here, would best build on the ideas presented in this paragraph and connect to the final sentence of the essay?
options: She loves when people, no matter what their ethnicity, wear traditional clothing every day.
She often teaches paj ntaub to Hmong adults her age who want to learn new techniques.
Recently, she worked with nine young Hmong women in a formal apprenticeship.
One of her own favorite pieces tells the story of her family.
questions.explain: The final sentence says Pang Xiong “is showing a new generation the joys of paj ntaub.” Option C (working with nine young Hmong women in an apprenticeship) directly builds on that idea of teaching a new generation. The others do not connect to the final sentence.

passages.title: Passage I — Kenji Nakamura and the Art of Kintsugi

paras.t: Morning light falls across shelves crowded with bowls awaiting repair, some shattered in earthquakes, others dropped at weddings.
In a Kyoto workshop, restorer Kenji Nakamura holds two halves of a
busted
tea bowl.
Instead of hiding the crack, he
will trace it in gold. This is kintsugi, the Japanese art of mending pottery with lacquer dusted in gold.
The bowl before him once belonged to a tea master in Uji, and its stain of green still marks the inner curve.
Urushi lacquer hardens only in humid air.
The sap is tapped from urushi trees in summer, then aged for years before it is fit for a brush.
Mixed with gold dust, Nakamura paints the seams.
Yet the philosophy runs deeper than decoration.
Kintsugi, which dates to fifteenth-century Japan, treats
breakage as history rather than flaw.
Legend traces the craft to a shogun who broke a favorite tea bowl and sent it to China for staples, only to receive it back bound in ugly metal clamps.
Nakamura works slowly. He
joins together
the shards with thin bamboo spatulas, then waits weeks between coats.
Each coat must cure in a damp cabinet, or the lacquer will wrinkle and peel.
The careful layering of lacquer, gold, and time produce
a seam stronger than the original clay. Apprentices spend their first year grinding pigments and cleaning brushes before they are allowed to touch a seam. A single bowl can require
a lot of time.
When the work is done, the bowl becomes
a way cooler object after getting smashed.
The wait, Nakamura says, is the real repair.
Collectors now like
mended pieces above flawless ones. The crack, once a flaw, becomes the biography.
Museums from Tokyo to New York now display mended bowls beside flawless ones, and students travel to Kyoto to study the craft. Prices at auction have risen with each passing decade.

passages.title: Passage II — The Axolotl's Second Chance

paras.t: In the canals of Xochimilco, near Mexico City, swims an animal that refuses to grow up. The axolotl, a salamander
that keeps its juvenile gills throughout its adult life,
can regrow entire limbs, jaws, and even
parts of it's heart.
Researchers
whom
study regeneration prize the axolotl above mice and zebrafish.
A severed limb regrows in weeks, complete with bone, muscle, and nerves.
In the wild, the axolotl is critically endangered.
Pollution and invasive tilapia have shrunk its canals to a fraction of their former range.

passages.title: Passage III — Night Train to Hue

paras.t: The Reunification Express runs the length of Vietnam, from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City, in thirty-six hours.
Hanoi station at ten at night is all steam and shouting. The platform
buzzes
with vendors selling tea and sticky rice. Porters shouldered canvas duffels, conductors blew sharp whistles, and a boy hawked lottery tickets along the cars.
Tea steam curled through air thick with coal smoke and star anise.
I found my sleeper car by its number, climbed the narrow ladder, and claimed the lower berth by the window.
My berthmate, a grandmother carrying two baskets of lychees, patted the bunk beside her. She peeled a lychee for me
, it burst sweet and cold on my tongue.
Juice ran down my chin, and she laughed until her shoulders shook.
She spoke no English, and my Vietnamese consisted of only two words, just hello and thank you.
We traded names through gestures, then sat in comfortable silence as the city lights thinned. Her baskets, I gathered, were bound for her daughter's market stall in Hue.
Somewhere past midnight,
the train's steady and regular rhythm finally slowed my thoughts.
The wheels kept a four-beat measure against the rails, steady as a resting pulse.
The villages flashing past the window, each a scatter of lamps,
recalls
scenes from films I had never seen. Rice paddies stretched silver under the moon, broken here and there by the dark humps of water buffalo.
I understood, suddenly, how far a single night could carry a person forward in their life.
Work emails, deadlines, the apartment hunt — all of it receded with the kilometer posts. I had boarded the train wound tight with city noise; somewhere past Ninh Binh, the knot loosened.
By dawn,
mist hung over the Perfume River. Fishermen poled flat boats through the shallows, their lanterns still burning.
I stepped onto the platform into air smelling of rain and frangipani. The platform loudspeakers crackled announcements I could not understand, and I followed the crowd toward the gate.

passages.title: Passage IV — The Case for School Gardens

paras.t: At Jefferson Elementary, the best classroom has no roof. The idea sounds quaint until the test scores arrive. Third-graders water seedlings before the morning bell, and sixth-graders compost lunch scraps at noon.
Schools should plant gardens, because growing food teaches science, patience, and responsibility better than any textbook.
Rows of lettuce and sunflowers border the playground blacktop. The program began with four raised beds; it now covers half an acre behind the gymnasium.
The case begins with learning. Teachers tie fractions to seed spacing and biology to pollination.
Last spring, students harvested 400 pounds of lettuce for the cafeteria.
Cafeteria staff plan menus around the harvest calendar, and food waste has fallen by a third.
Students learn patience by
digging, planting, and to harvest.
However, test scores rose in every participating grade.
Every school that joins the program receives
their
own beds. A district grant pays for soil, tools, and a part-time garden coordinator.
Critics call gardens a distraction from tested subjects. Why dig, they ask, when the test is in May? Principals worry about instructional minutes, and some parents question muddy shoes.
Yet no lesson holds attention like one you can eat.
Attendance improves on garden days, and nurses report fewer afternoon stomachaches.
The work depends on volunteers. Grandparents build trellises, teenagers log service hours, and local nurseries donate seedlings.
The results speak plainly: higher scores, calmer hallways, fuller plates.
Suspensions have dropped, and teachers say focus lasts longer after outdoor lessons.
In short, the garden teaches what no worksheet can.
The model has spread to forty schools across the county.
The blacktop classroom is enrolling new students every spring. Each spring, the waiting list for garden plots grows longer than the one for the soccer team.

passages.title: Passage V — The Crows of Sendai

paras.t: At intersections in Sendai, Japan, carrion crows have learned to eat what the traffic cracks open. A crow drops a walnut into the crosswalk and waits on a lamppost while cars do the crushing.
It swoops down during the red light to collect the kernel.
Each nut, positioned at the lane's edge where tires pass most often, cracks cleanly.
Young crows learn the routine by watching elders, not by instinct alone.
Neither the horns nor the waiting
seem
to bother them.
Biologists rank the feat with tool use.
A crow that cannot crack a nut goes hungry, but a crow that reads a traffic light eats.

passages.title: Passage VI — Amara Diallo and the Talking Drums

paras.t: He stretches goatskin over carved lenke wood, tunes it with iron rings and rope, and
coaxes speech from a drum.

Amara Diallo is a master of the tama, the hourglass talking drum of West Africa. In the Diallo family, drum-making stretches back four generations to his great-grandfather, a griot who played for village ceremonies. He selects each hide by touch, rejecting any skin too thin to hold a tone. His workshop smells of hide glue and shea oil.
No drum speaks
more clearly than any instrument in the ensemble.

Squeezing the ropes bends the pitch; striking the head releases it. A skilled player can praise a chief, warn of danger, or tease a friend, all without a single word. Court drummers once carried news between villages faster than any runner.
Diallo performs with symphony orchestras and hip-hop artists alike.
Critics who once dismissed the tama as folk craft now review his concerts alongside classical recitals.
He builds drums with shells, goatskin heads, and iron tuning rings
(usually carved from a single lenke log).
Because Yoruba is a tonal language, the drum can mimic its rises and falls.
Children learning Yoruba sometimes practice tones on small practice drums before they can read. The drum, players say, simply speaks the language aloud.
Apprentices begin as children. A beginner spends months squeezing rope patterns in silence before striking a single note. Years of practice
effect
the player's fluency. Diallo dislikes hearing his drums called
simple
instruments. Fame has taken Diallo to concert halls on four continents.
Therefore,
he still teaches beginners in Bamako each summer. His oldest students now teach beginners of their own.
Each student carves
their
first drumstick before touching a drumhead.
Diallo is passing the drum's language to a new generation. As long as children gather to listen, he says, the drum will never fall silent.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The opening contrast — hiding versus tracing in gold — must stay intact. B reverses the meaning into hiding, C splices two clauses with a comma, and D deletes the contrast the sentence is built on.

questions.stem: The writer wants to describe the bowl precisely while maintaining the essay's formal tone. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
questions.explain: "Shattered" precisely means broken into fragments, fitting a bowl in two halves. "Busted" is slang, "broken" is vaguer, and "destroyed" overstates damage to a bowl about to be repaired.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: Mixed with gold dust, Nakamura, painting the seams,
Painting the seams, Nakamura mixes the gold dust.
Mixed with gold dust, the seams are painted by Nakamura.
questions.explain: The opener describes the lacquer on the seams, so the subject must be the seams — only D supplies it. A attaches the mixture to the man, C is grammatical but reverses the process by mixing after painting begins, and B leaves the sentence without a main verb.

questions.stem: Given that all the choices are accurate, which one provides the best transition from technique to meaning?
questions.explain: The paragraph moves from lacquer technique to the philosophy behind it, and "yet the philosophy runs deeper" bridges exactly that shift. B and C state true but unbridging facts, and D contradicts the weeks-long curing the essay establishes.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: that dates to fifteenth-century Japan, treats
which dates to fifteenth-century Japan treats
questions.explain: The history is non-essential — there is one kintsugi — so it needs "which" with paired commas. "That" cannot take a comma, and C and D drop the closing comma the aside requires.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively maintains the essay's formal tone?
options: more precious for having been broken.
questions.explain: "More precious for having been broken" states the wabi-sabi idea in the essay's formal register. The original leans on slang ("way cooler," "smashed"), and B and D stay casual.

questions.stem: Which choice is least redundant in context?
questions.explain: "Join" already means to bring together, so B says it once. A restates it, C triples it, and D swaps in a synonym without removing the restatement.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The subject is the singular "layering" — cross out "of lacquer, gold, and time" — so the verb must be "produces." A, B, and C all give plural or mismatched verbs to a singular subject.

questions.stem: The writer wants to give a concrete sense of the patience the craft requires. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: a month of drying between coats.
questions.explain: A month of drying between coats quantifies the patience; "a lot of time" and "an enjoyable hobby" stay vague, and "a quick afternoon" contradicts the slow process.

questions.stem: The writer wants a closing verb that captures cherishing, not merely purchasing. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
questions.explain: "Treasure" means to cherish, which is the essay's whole point about mended bowls. "Like" is too weak for the closing claim, "hoard" turns cherishing sinister, and "buy" shrinks the idea to commerce.

questions.stem: The writer wants to introduce the axolotl's defining trait. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
questions.explain: Keeping juvenile gills into adulthood — neoteny — is the trait the essay is about. B says nothing distinctive, C twists neoteny into agelessness, and D invents a refusal to eat.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The animal is singular, so the possessive must be "its" with no apostrophe. "It's" means "it is," "their" mismatches the singular animal, and "its'" is not a word.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The pronoun performs the verb "study," so the subject form "who" is required. "Whom" is the objective case, "which" is for things rather than researchers, and "whose" is possessive.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state the remarkable fact behind the axolotl's fame. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: A severed limb regrows in seconds.
A severed limb regrows only in winter.
questions.explain: Weeks-long regrowth complete with bone, muscle, and nerves is the measured marvel. A contradicts it, C compresses weeks into seconds, and D invents a seasonal condition.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state the wild axolotl's threat concretely. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: Invasive tilapia have improved the canals.
questions.explain: Pollution plus invasive tilapia shrinking the canals names the concrete threat. A contradicts the endangered status, B states a vacuous fact, and D reverses the tilapia's harm into help.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The memoir is told in the past tense, so the simple past "buzzed" is required. A shifts into the present, C tangles past perfect with future, and D leaves the clause with no main verb.

questions.stem: The writer wants to open with a vivid sensory portrait of the station. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: Tea steam, coal smoke, and star anise were present.
questions.explain: Tea steam curling through coal smoke and star anise lets the reader smell the platform. B states a vacuous fact, C stays flat, and D lists the same ingredients while killing the image.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: it burst sweet and cold on my tongue.
, bursting sweet and cold on my tongue.
; it burst sweet and cold on my tongue.
questions.explain: Two complete clauses need a semicolon between them, as in D. A splices them with a comma, B fuses them with no punctuation, and C strands "bursting" so it appears the narrator bursts.

questions.stem: Which choice is least redundant in context?
options: She spoke no English, and my Vietnamese consisted of only two words, just hello and thank you and nothing else.
She spoke no English, and my Vietnamese consisted of two words: hello and thank you.
She spoke no English, and my Vietnamese consisted of hello and thank you words.
questions.explain: "Only" and "just" restate each other, so C says it once with a clean colon. B triples the restatement, and D mangles the phrasing into nonsense.

questions.stem: Which choice is least redundant in context?
options: the train's steady rhythm finally slowed my thoughts.
the train's steady and regular rhythm finally slowed my thoughts right down.
questions.explain: "Steady" and "regular" say the same thing, so B keeps one. C pads the restatement further, and D drops the reflection the sentence exists to deliver.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The subject is the plural "villages" — "each a scatter of lamps" is only a parenthetical — so the verb must be "recall." A follows the singular "each," B breaks the past-tense frame, and C leaves no main verb.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state the midnight realization as compactly as possible. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: I understood, suddenly, how far one night could carry a person.
I understood, suddenly, how trains have engines.
I understood, suddenly, how late it was.
questions.explain: B keeps the realization and cuts the padding ("single," "forward in their life"). C states a mechanical vacuity, and D flattens the moment into clock-watching.

questions.stem: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?
options: Nevertheless, mist hung over the Perfume River.
For example, mist hung over the Perfume River.
Instead, mist hung over the Perfume River.
questions.explain: "By dawn" correctly advances the clock from midnight to arrival. "Nevertheless" and "instead" signal contrasts that never come, and "for example" frames an arrival as an illustration.

questions.stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following accurate sentence: *My berthmate pressed a bag of lychees into my hands as I stepped onto the platform.* Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it completes the berthmate's farewell at the arrival moment.
Yes, because it proves that lychees grow in Hue.
No, because it shifts focus to train mechanics.
No, because it denies the berthmate existed.
questions.explain: The pressed bag of lychees closes the berthmate thread exactly where she leaves the story. B overclaims Hue agriculture, C misreads farewell as mechanics, and D reverses two paragraphs of her company.

questions.stem: *Question 25 asks about the preceding passage as a whole.* The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *I have never slept so well.* The sentence would most logically be placed at:
questions.explain: The sleep claim belongs with the midnight reflection, where the rhythm slows the narrator's thoughts. Point A is departure bustle, Point B the berthmate scene, and Point D the dawn arrival.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state the essay's central argument in formal language. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: Schools should plant a ton of gardens because dirt is awesome.
Jefferson Elementary should plant one tomato.
questions.explain: A states the position plainly and previews the essay's case: science, patience, and responsibility, better than any textbook. B slips into slang, C is true but off-thesis, and D narrows a national argument to one tomato.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: to dig, to plant, and to harvest.
questions.explain: After "by," the series needs matching gerunds: digging, planting, harvesting. A mixes in an infinitive, C's infinitives cannot follow "by," and D mixes bare verbs with an infinitive.

questions.stem: The writer wants to show the garden's cafeteria impact with concrete evidence. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: Last spring, students napped in the garden.
Last spring, students harvested four lettuce leaves.
questions.explain: Four hundred pounds of cafeteria lettuce proves impact directly. A naps through the point, B floods it, and C shrinks the harvest to a garnish.

questions.stem: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?
options: As a result, test scores rose in every participating grade.
For example, test scores rose in every participating grade.
Instead, test scores rose in every participating grade.
questions.explain: Rising scores are presented as a result of the garden program, so "as a result" is required. "However" and "instead" signal contrasts that never come, and "for example" misframes a result as an illustration.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The antecedent is the singular "every school," so the possessive must be "its." "Their" mismatches the singular, "there" names a place, and "they're" means "they are."

questions.stem: The writer wants to answer the critics by naming what only a garden can teach. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: Yet gardens are prettier than classrooms.
Yet critics should visit a farm.
Yet tests matter more than tomatoes.
questions.explain: An edible lesson answers the distraction charge head-on: attention you can eat. A retreats to prettiness, B dismisses the critics rudely, and D surrenders to the testing regime.

questions.stem: At this point, the writer is considering adding the following accurate sentence: *Retired neighbors teach composting on Saturdays.* Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it names the community help the volunteer work depends on.
Yes, because it proves that every retiree gardens.
No, because it shifts focus to school athletics.
No, because it denies that volunteers matter.
questions.explain: Saturday compost lessons are the concrete community help the paragraph's volunteer work requires. B overgeneralizes to every retiree, C misreads compost as athletics, and D reverses the sentence into denial.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: The results speak plainly; higher scores, calmer hallways, fuller plates.
The results speak plainly, higher scores, calmer hallways, fuller plates.
The results speak plainly higher scores, calmer hallways, fuller plates.
questions.explain: The colon correctly follows a complete sentence and introduces the elaborating list. A semicolon cannot introduce a list, a comma splices it into the clause, and no punctuation fuses them together.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the paragraph by returning to the essay's central contrast?
options: In short, test scores are everything.
questions.explain: The garden-versus-worksheet contrast restates the thesis in the paragraph's own terms. A overclaims worksheets' worthlessness, B replaces teachers the essay never dismisses, and C crowns the testing regime the essay argues against.

questions.stem: *Question 35 asks about the preceding passage as a whole.* The writer wants to add the following sentence to the essay: *A waiting list of parent volunteers grows every semester.* The sentence would most logically be placed at:
questions.explain: The volunteer detail joins the community paragraph, where the work depends on volunteers. Point A introduces the thesis, Point B presents evidence and results, and Point D closes on outcomes.

questions.stem: If the writer were to delete the phrase “where tires pass most often” from the preceding sentence (adjusting the punctuation as needed), the sentence would primarily lose:
options: specific information that explains why the lane's edge cracks nuts reliably.
specific information that gives the walnut's weight in grams.
details that prove crows invented the crosswalk.
details that describe the lamppost's height.
questions.explain: The phrase locates the nuts where tires pass most often — the reason the edge cracks them reliably. B invents a weight, C credits crows with inventing crosswalks, and D looks up at the wrong object.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state the crow's learned safety rule. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: It swoops down into speeding traffic to collect the kernel.
It flies south for the winter.
questions.explain: Waiting for the red light is the learned rule that keeps the crow alive. A reverses it into suicide, B migrates out of the story, and D scrambles the drop-wait-collect sequence.

questions.stem: The writer wants to state how young crows acquire the routine. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
options: Young crows hatch knowing the full routine.
Young crows prefer lampposts to trees.
questions.explain: Watching elders — not instinct alone — is the essay's learning mechanism. A hatches them pre-trained, C cuts the teachers out, and D compares furniture irrelevantly.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: With "neither/nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject: the singular "waiting" needs "seems." The plural "horns" lures readers toward A, while C and D break the construction entirely.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively closes the passage on the essay's central irony?
options: Traffic lights exist to feed crows.
questions.explain: A crow reading a traffic light to eat is the irony the whole passage earns. A reverses the lights' purpose, B compares diets irrelevantly, and C contradicts three paragraphs of walnut-cracking.

questions.stem: The writer wants to open with the craft's marvel in vivid language. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
questions.explain: "Coaxes speech from a drum" states the talking-drum marvel the whole essay explores. B and C flatten it to vacant thumping, and D mistakes the drum for furniture.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
options: more clearer than any instrument in the ensemble.
most clearly than any instrument in the ensemble.
more clearly than any other instrument in the ensemble.
questions.explain: The drum must be excluded from its own comparison with "other." A doubles the comparative, B mixes a superlative with "than," and C compares the drum to itself.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
options: Kept, because it proves orchestras replace griots.
Deleted, because it detracts from ancient styles.
Kept, because it places the tradition in a modern context.
Deleted, because it is irrelevant to drumming.
questions.explain: Symphonies and hip-hop show the tradition alive today — the modern context the essay needs. A overclaims replacement, while B and D wrongly call living proof irrelevant.

questions.stem: The best placement for the underlined portion would be:
questions.explain: Only the shells are carved from a log, so the parenthetical belongs after "shells." Where it sits now it attaches to the iron rings, after "drums" it stays ambiguous, and after "heads" it claims goatskin is carved.

questions.stem: The writer wants to explain why the drum can mimic speech. Which choice best accomplishes that goal?
questions.explain: Tonal rises and falls are the mechanism the sentence must state. A offers volume without meaning, B invents memorized speeches, and C denies the language words it plainly has.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: As a verb, "effect" means to bring about — years of practice bring about fluency — so "effect" is correct. "Affect" means merely to influence, C leaves no main verb, and D shifts into the present tense.

questions.stem: The writer is considering revising the underlined portion to the following: *primitive* Should the writer make this revision?
options: Yes, because “primitive” praises the drums' age.
No, because “primitive” insults a tradition the essay honors.
No, because the drums are electronic.
questions.explain: “Primitive” insults the mastery the essay celebrates; the revision must be refused. A misreads insult as praise, B invents a grammar error, and D hallucinates electronics.

questions.stem: Which transition word or phrase is most logical in context?
questions.explain: Global fame against village teaching is a contrast, so "however" is required. "Therefore" claims the teaching results from the fame, "for example" misframes it as illustration, and "meanwhile" claims simultaneity the sentence never establishes.

questions.stem: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.explain: The antecedent is the singular "each student," so the pronoun must be "his or her." "Their" mismatches the singular, "its" is for things rather than students, and "there" names a place.

questions.stem: Which of the following true statements, if added here, would best build on the ideas presented in this paragraph and connect to the final sentence of the essay?
options: Last year, twelve of his students performed at the national arts festival, proving festivals replace lessons.
Last year, twelve kora players performed at the national arts festival.
Last year, twelve of his students performed at the national arts festival.
Last year, Diallo stopped teaching entirely.
questions.explain: Twelve students on a festival stage show the new generation carrying the drum's language forward. A overclaims replacement, B swaps in the wrong instrument, and D reverses a lifetime of teaching.
